title: Classification of high-dimensional data with spiked covariance matrix structure

strengths: The paper addresses an identifiable audience interested in high-dimensional classification with strong correlations. Sparsity of the whitened mean difference provides a useful alternative to sparsity of the original discriminant direction.

The whitening, screening, and classification procedure is straightforward. The connections to CAT-LDA and rotation-based classifiers are informative, and entrywise perturbation analysis is well motivated for studying support recovery.

The experiments cover three covariance settings, relevant competing methods, 200 Monte Carlo replications with separate test samples, and two gene-expression datasets. The reported results provide encouraging evidence of competitive classification, particularly in the random-factor setting.
weaknesses: Necessary—eigenvalue assumptions: The principal guarantees are not established under the stated conditions. Condition 3 assumes only λk = O(p), which does not imply diverging spikes, bounded effective rank, or comparable spike sizes. For example, Σ = I + uuᵀ with u = 1/√p has bounded coherence and satisfies this condition, but its effective rank is (p+1)/2. The appendix nevertheless uses stronger eigenvalue scaling and comparability, including in (B.15) and Lemma 2. State sufficient lower bounds or eigengap assumptions and recheck the proofs under those assumptions.

Necessary—consistency proof: Theorem 3 assumes log p = o(n), whereas Appendix B.4 concludes using log n · log p = o(n). Its displayed bound involving √(log n · log p/n) does not vanish throughout the claimed regime. A sharper argument establishing almost-sure convergence of conditional risk, or a narrower theorem statement, is needed.

Necessary—adaptivity: Section 2.3 claims consistent estimation of both d and s, but the theorems use the true spike count d and establish no guarantee for its estimator. The experimental 90% explained-variance rule is generally inconsistent for spike counting: in Model 1 with ρ = 0.5, there is one spike, but the population rule retains approximately 0.8p components. Provide a justified rank estimator and corresponding analysis, or restrict the theoretical claims to known d and identify the experimental rule as a heuristic.

Necessary—elliptical extension: Section 5.1 incorrectly asserts that the Gaussian Fisher rule remains Bayes optimal for general common-covariance elliptical distributions with arbitrary class priors. The likelihood ratio involves log h(q1) − log h(q2), which generally does not give the Gaussian linear boundary when priors are unequal. Sub-Gaussian tails do not resolve this issue. Restrict the extension appropriately, such as to equal priors and a common decreasing radial density, or derive and analyze the correct decision rule.

Necessary—mathematical specification: Equation (3.1) uses −||ζ||²/2 inside Φ; the Gaussian error formula requires −||ζ||/2. Also, Section 2.3 defines Λ̂ as the leading sample covariance eigenvalues, which already estimate λk + σ², but adds σ̂² again when constructing D̂. Resolve this inconsistency and clarify which estimator was implemented, since the formulas currently do not specify the intended whitening consistently.

Necessary—experimental accuracy: Several statements overstate the tables: PCLDA does not have the highest accuracy throughout Model 1, and Table 11 contradicts the statement that it retains all strong signals. Table 2 also repeats several entries between ρ = 0.7 and 0.8. For the specified model at ρ = 0.8, the analytical Bayes error is approximately 0.022%, whereas the reported oracle average is 0.19%. Audit the results and align the discussion with the verified findings.

Necessary—feature-count interpretation: Although Section 2.2 distinguishes raw and whitened coordinates, the model-size comparisons need that distinction carried into their interpretation. Selecting s whitened coordinates generally produces a dense classifier in the original variables and still requires those variables to compute the transformation. The evidence supports a compact transformed representation, rather than directly establishing comparable reductions in measured genes or original-variable support.

Optional improvements: Experiments varying sample size, dimension, and rank selection would help connect the finite-sample results to the theory. A simulation satisfying exact whitened sparsity and a CAT-LDA comparison on the real datasets would also be informative. These additions are secondary to correcting the guarantees and reported evidence above.
